title: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
summary: Why one-hot codes fail, how word2vec learns vectors from context, training it yourself, evaluating and plotting embeddings, ID embeddings with hashing, and contrastive learning without collapse.
outcomes: Explain why one-hot codes cannot share knowledge between related items and how an embedding lookup fixes it
Compute one skip-gram negative sampling update by hand and train the same model in PyTorch and gensim
Explain what cosine neighbours and vector analogies do and do not show, including the shifted PMI view and GloVe
Evaluate an embedding with Spearman correlation and read PCA and t-SNE plots without the common misreadings
Design ID embeddings for large or open catalogs with supervised training, hashing and an unknown row
Explain how subword vectors, contextual vectors and bias tests address the failures of static word vectors
Compute InfoNCE and NT-Xent losses at different temperatures and explain why negatives prevent collapse

lessons.title: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table

blocks.md: In the prerequisite course you trained networks whose inputs were numbers. Words, product IDs, user IDs and other *categorical* inputs are not numbers, so the first question is how to feed them to a network at all. The simplest answer is a **one-hot vector**: give each of the $W$ items in the vocabulary an index, and represent item $i$ as a length-$W$ vector that is all zeros except a 1 at position $i$.

Take a vocabulary of five words: *cat, dog, kitten, car, truck*. One-hot coding gives *cat* = `[1,0,0,0,0]` and *kitten* = `[0,0,1,0,0]`. Every word is exactly as far from every other word. The dot product between any two different one-hot vectors is 0, so their **cosine similarity** (the dot product divided by the two lengths, ranging from -1 to 1) is also 0.

blocks.prompt: A sentiment model has learned from training data that *cat* tends to appear in positive reviews. With one-hot inputs, how much of that knowledge transfers to *kitten*, which never appeared in training?
blocks.reveal: **None.** The weights that multiply the *cat* input position are separate from the weights for the *kitten* position, and nothing ties them together. One-hot coding tells the network that *cat* and *kitten* are as unrelated as *cat* and *truck*. Every word must be learned from its own examples, which fails for rare words. Bengio et al. (2003) proposed learned word vectors to fight this, as part of what they call the curse of dimensionality: test word sequences differ from every sequence seen in training. Each extra word multiplies the number of possible sequences by the vocabulary size: 10 words from a 100,000-word vocabulary give $10^{50}$ sequences, far more than any corpus holds.

blocks.title: Cosine similarity: one-hot codes vs dense vectors

scenes.caption: One-hot codes: each word is similar only to itself. The off-diagonal is all 0, so the representation carries no notion of related words.
Dense 3-dimensional vectors (toy values chosen by hand to mimic trained ones). Now cat and kitten score 0.99 and cat and car score -0.39: similar words sit close together.
The two blocks are the animals and the vehicles. A model that learns something about cat now gets a head start on kitten (0.99) and a little on dog (0.8).

blocks.md: An **embedding** is that dense vector: each item gets a row of $d$ real numbers, with $d$ much smaller than $W$ (often tens to a few hundred). Stacking the rows gives an **embedding matrix** $E$ of shape $W \times d$. Bengio et al. (2003) introduced exactly this for neural language models: a $|V| \times m$ matrix $C$ (their $|V|$ and $m$ are this course's $W$ and $d$) of free parameters whose row $i$ is the feature vector of word $i$, learned jointly with the rest of the network.

Looking up a row is the same as multiplying the one-hot vector by $E$. The one-hot vector selects one row and zeros out the others, so the network never has to do the full multiplication. Frameworks implement the lookup directly: PyTorch's `nn.Embedding(num_embeddings, embedding_dim)` is documented as "a simple lookup table" whose `weight` has shape `(num_embeddings, embedding_dim)` and is initialized from $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$. That symbol is the standard normal distribution, the bell curve with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so every entry starts as a random number, about 95 percent of them between -2 and 2.

blocks.caption: Multiplying by a one-hot vector selects row 2 (0-based) of the embedding matrix.

blocks.title: An embedding lookup selects rows of E

scenes.caption: The embedding matrix E: 5 words by 3 dimensions, 15 trainable numbers. In a real model they start random and training moves them.
Input token kitten (index 2): the lookup returns row 2, [0.9, 0.0, 0.4]. This is identical to one-hot times E, without the 12 multiplications by zero.
A batch of tokens [cat, car, cat] reads rows 0, 3 and 0. Rows 1, 2 and 4 are untouched by this batch, so they receive zero gradient in the backward pass.

blocks.md: Because an embedding is just a weight matrix, backpropagation trains it like any other layer: the gradient of the loss with respect to a looked-up row is the gradient flowing into that row's output, and rows that were not looked up get exactly zero. That sparsity is why PyTorch offers `sparse=True`, which returns a sparse gradient; its docs note that only some optimizers support it (`optim.SGD`, `optim.SparseAdam`, and `optim.Adagrad` on CPU). Here SGD is the plain gradient step from the prerequisite course. Adagrad and Adam are optimizers that give every parameter its own step size from running statistics of its past gradients (Adagrad divides by the square root of the summed squared gradients, Adam keeps moving averages of the gradient and of its square), and SparseAdam is PyTorch's masked version of Adam that updates those statistics only for the rows present in the sparse gradient.

The memory cost is $W \times d$ numbers. A 50,000-word vocabulary with $d = 300$ is 15,000,000 parameters, so embedding tables are often the largest single layer in models that handle large vocabularies or catalogs of IDs.

An embedding is a learned weight matrix indexed by item ID. Meaning is not built in: the vectors start random and become useful only because some training objective rewards putting related items close together. The rest of this course is about which objectives do that.

blocks.question: A batch contains the token IDs [2, 2, 4] and the model uses an embedding table with 5 rows. After one backward pass, which rows of the table have a nonzero gradient?
options: All 5 rows, because the whole matrix is a parameter
Rows 2 and 4, with row 2's gradient being the sum of two contributions
Rows 2 and 4, with row 2's gradient counted once because duplicates are removed
Only row 4, because repeated tokens cancel out
blocks.explain: Only looked-up rows get gradient, and a row looked up twice accumulates both contributions (the lookup's backward pass is a scatter-add: each position's gradient is added into the row its ID points to, so repeats sum). Rows 0, 1 and 3 get exactly zero, which is what makes sparse updates possible.

blocks.question: Why do the dense vectors let a model generalize from cat to kitten when one-hot codes do not?
options: Dense vectors have more dimensions, so they hold more information
The dot product of two one-hot vectors is undefined
Nearby inputs produce nearby activations, so what the network learned for one word partly applies to the other
Dense vectors are normalized to length 1
blocks.explain: The downstream layers are smooth functions of their input. If kitten's vector is close to cat's, the network's output for kitten is close to its output for cat. One-hot codes have more dimensions, not fewer, and their dot products are well defined (just always 0).

lessons.title: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours

blocks.md: Where does a training signal for *cat is like kitten* come from without labels? The **distributional hypothesis** (Harris, 1954) says that words occurring in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. *Cat* and *kitten* both show up near *purr*, *fed*, *the*, *litter*. If we train vectors to predict a word's neighbours, words with similar neighbours are pushed toward similar vectors.

**Skip-gram**, from Mikolov et al. (2013) and released as the word2vec (word to vector) tool, turns that into a prediction task. Slide over text. At each position the word there is the *center* word, and every word within $c$ positions on either side is a *context* word. Each (center, context) pair is a training example: given the center, predict the context. These pairs give the method its name: a skip-gram is a pair (more generally an n-gram) of words that may have other words skipped between them.

blocks.md: Each word gets **two** vectors: an *input* vector $v_w$, used when the word is the center, and an *output* vector $u_w$, used when it is a context. Both are rows of embedding matrices of shape $W \times d$. The original skip-gram scores a context word $o$ for center word $c$ (from here on $c$ names the center word, not the window size, as in the usual notation) with a softmax over the whole vocabulary:

blocks.caption: Skip-gram softmax (Mikolov et al., 2013b, eq. 2, with v as input and u as output vectors): e to the score of the pair (o, c), divided by the sum of e to the score of every word w with c. Training maximizes the average log of this over all pairs.

blocks.md: This is a **softmax**: it turns $W$ raw scores into probabilities. Taking $\exp$ of each score makes it positive without changing the order, and dividing by the sum over all words makes the results add up to 1, so a word whose output vector points the same way as $v_c$ gets a large share. Maximizing the log of it raises the true context's score and, through the denominator, lowers every other word's.

blocks.prompt: For one training pair, how many dot products does the softmax denominator need if the vocabulary has 1,000,000 words?
blocks.reveal: **All 1,000,000**, one per vocabulary word, and the gradient touches every output vector. Mikolov et al. note that the cost of the gradient of $\log p(w_O \mid w_I)$ (their notation for $p(o \mid c)$: the output word given the input word) is proportional to $W$, which is often $10^5$ to $10^7$. With billions of pairs this is far too slow, which is the problem the next lesson's negative sampling solves.

blocks.title: Skip-gram: full softmax vs negative sampling

scenes.caption: The center word's ID selects its input vector v_cat. Output vectors u_w live in a second table.
Full softmax: every one of the W output vectors is dotted with v_cat and normalized. Cost per pair grows with the vocabulary size.
Negative sampling (next lesson): only the true context and k sampled noise words are scored, each with an independent sigmoid. With k = 5 that is 6 dot products instead of W.

blocks.md: The full softmax costs $W$ dot products per prediction, and Mikolov et al. (2013b) describe two cheaper replacements. One is negative sampling, the next lesson. The other is **hierarchical softmax** (first used for neural language models by Morin and Bengio): put the $W$ words at the leaves of a binary tree and replace the single $W$-way choice by a walk from the root to the word's leaf. Each inner node of the tree has its own vector and makes one left-or-right decision with a sigmoid, and a word's probability is the product of the decisions on its path, so only about $\log_2 W$ nodes are evaluated. word2vec builds the tree as a Huffman tree, which gives frequent words short paths. Libraries expose the choice as a switch; in gensim it is `hs=1` together with `negative=0` (with both on, gensim trains both objectives at once).

Skip-gram is not trained to be a good language model; the prediction task is a pretext. Mikolov et al. say plainly that the skip-gram model is only concerned with learning high-quality vector representations. After training, the output layer is usually thrown away and the input vectors are kept as the embeddings.

A sibling architecture, **CBOW** (continuous bag of words, from the same 2013 paper), flips the direction: it averages the input vectors of the context words and predicts the center word from that average. *Bag of words* means the order of the context words is ignored; *continuous* means each context word is a dense vector rather than a count. Mikolov et al. describe it as projecting every context word into the same position, so their vectors are averaged. With $m$ context words on each side of position $t$:

blocks.tex: h_t = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{\substack{-m \le j \le m \\ j \ne 0}} v_{w_{t+j}}, \qquad p(w_t \mid \text{context}) = \frac{\exp(u_{w_t}^\top h_t)}{\sum_{w=1}^{W} \exp(u_w^\top h_t)}
blocks.caption: CBOW: h_t is the average of the 2m context words' input vectors; the center word w_t is scored with its output vector against h_t, through the same softmax skip-gram uses.

blocks.md: Both rely on the same idea: the only supervision is the text itself, so any large corpus (a collection of text) becomes training data. This is the first example of **self-supervised** representation learning in this course.

blocks.question: With window $c = 2$, how many (center, context) pairs does the 6-word sentence *the cat sat on the mat* produce?
blocks.explain: Edge words have fewer neighbours: positions 0 and 5 get 2 context words each, positions 1 and 4 get 3, positions 2 and 3 get 4. That is 2 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 18. The naive 6 x 4 = 24 forgets that the window is cut off at the sentence edges.

blocks.question: Two words, *Paris* and *Rome*, never appear in the same sentence in the training corpus. Can skip-gram still give them similar vectors?
options: No, they must co-occur to be pulled together
Yes, if they share many context words such as city, capital and visited
Only if they are in the same window at least once
Only with CBOW, not skip-gram
blocks.explain: Similarity comes from shared contexts, not direct co-occurrence. Both input vectors are trained to score highly against the same output vectors (u_city, u_capital, ...), which pushes them toward the same region of the space.

blocks.question: A balanced binary tree holds a vocabulary of $W = 1{,}048{,}576 = 2^{20}$ words at its leaves. How many sigmoid decisions does hierarchical softmax make to score one word?
blocks.explain: The path from the root to a leaf in a balanced tree of $2^{20}$ leaves has 20 inner nodes, one sigmoid each, instead of a million dot products. A Huffman tree is not balanced: frequent words get shorter paths and rare words longer ones, which lowers the average cost on real text.

lessons.title: Negative sampling: one word2vec update by hand

blocks.md: Negative sampling replaces the $W$-way softmax with a much cheaper question: *is this (center, context) pair real, or noise?* For each real pair, draw $k$ **negative** words from a noise distribution $P_n$ (a probability distribution over the vocabulary used to pick fake context words; its exact form comes below) and train a logistic classifier to say yes to the real pair and no to each negative. Mikolov et al. (2013b) define the objective for one pair, to be maximized, as:

blocks.caption: Skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS): log sigma of the real pair's score, plus log sigma of minus the score for each of k noise words drawn from P_n. Here sigma(x) = 1/(1+exp(-x)) and sigma(-x) = 1 - sigma(x). In training the expectation is replaced by k samples.

blocks.md: This is just the binary cross-entropy you know from logistic regression, applied to dot products. Read the sigmoid of a pair's score as the classifier's probability that the pair is real. The real pair has label 1 and costs minus the log of the sigmoid of its score; each negative has label 0 and costs minus the log of 1 minus the sigmoid of its score, which equals minus the log of the sigmoid of minus its score. The sum of these costs is minus the objective. Its gradients are short. They follow from two derivatives and the chain rule: minus the log of $\sigma(x)$ has slope $\sigma(x) - 1$, minus the log of $\sigma(-x)$ has slope $\sigma(x)$, and the dot product $u^\top v$ changes by $v$ per unit of $u$ and by $u$ per unit of $v$. With $s_o = \sigma(u_o^\top v_c)$ and $s_i = \sigma(u_{w_i}^\top v_c)$, the loss $L$ (the negative of the objective) has $\partial L/\partial u_o = (s_o - 1)\, v_c$, $\partial L/\partial u_{w_i} = s_i\, v_c$, and $\partial L/\partial v_c = (s_o - 1)\, u_o + \sum_i s_i\, u_{w_i}$.

Read the signs: the real context vector moves *toward* $v_c$, each negative moves *away*, and $v_c$ moves toward $u_o$ and away from the negatives. Let us do one step by hand with $d = 2$, center *cat*, real context *sat*, one negative *car* ($k = 1$), and learning rate 0.5. The starting vectors are small, as after random initialization.

blocks.title: One SGNS update for the pair (cat, sat)
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
sig = lambda x: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))
v = np.array([0.2, 0.1])       # input vector of cat
u_pos = np.array([0.3, -0.1])  # output vector of sat (real context)
u_neg = np.array([0.4, 0.3])   # output vector of car (noise sample)
lr = 0.5

s_pos = sig(u_pos @ v)   # model's P(real) for (cat, sat)
s_neg = sig(u_neg @ v)   # model's P(real) for (cat, car)
loss = -np.log(s_pos) - np.log(1 - s_neg)

g_v = (s_pos - 1) * u_pos + s_neg * u_neg
g_pos = (s_pos - 1) * v
g_neg = s_neg * v

v, u_pos, u_neg = v - lr * g_v, u_pos - lr * g_pos, u_neg - lr * g_neg
print(sig(u_pos @ v), sig(u_neg @ v))

scenes.caption: Start: three 2-d vectors. Only these three rows of the two tables take part in this step; the other W - 3 rows are untouched.
Scores: u_pos . v = 0.05 and u_neg . v = 0.11. Both sigmoids are near 0.5: the untrained model cannot tell the real pair from noise.
Loss = -ln(0.512) - ln(1 - 0.527) = 1.418. Two coin flips cost 2 ln 2 = 1.386, so we start slightly worse than chance.
Gradients. g_pos is negative (u_pos should move along +v), g_neg is positive (u_neg should move along -v).
SGD step: subtract lr times each gradient. Every update used the old values, computed before the assignment.
Re-score: P(real) for (cat, sat) rose to 0.515 and for (cat, car) fell to 0.514. Loss is now 1.386. Small steps, right direction.

scenes.caption: Step 5: 0.556 vs 0.471, loss 1.224. Progress is slow while the vectors are tiny, because each gradient is scaled by the other vectors' small entries.
Step 10: 0.846 vs 0.177, loss 0.361. Once the vectors grow, each step makes a bigger difference.
Step 20: 0.981 vs 0.021, loss 0.041. Simplified: real training interleaves billions of different pairs with fresh negatives, so no single pair is fit this hard.

blocks.md: **Which negatives?** Mikolov et al. tried several noise distributions and found that the unigram distribution raised to the 3/4 power, $P_n(w) = U(w)^{3/4}/Z$, significantly outperformed both the plain unigram and the uniform distribution. The unigram distribution $U(w)$ is each word's share of all tokens (word occurrences) in the corpus, counting single words on their own, and $Z$ is the sum of $U(w)^{3/4}$ over the vocabulary, which makes the new values add up to 1. Raising to 3/4 flattens the distribution: very frequent words are sampled a bit less and rare words a bit more. A word 1,000 times more frequent than another is drawn only about 178 times as often, because 1,000 to the power 3/4 is about 178. For $k$ they report 5 to 20 as useful for small datasets and as few as 2 to 5 for large ones.

blocks.title: Noise distribution for a toy corpus of 1,080 tokens

scenes.caption: Plain unigram: the would be 0.926 of all negatives, so most negative samples would teach almost nothing new.
Unigram to the 3/4: the drops to 0.84 while mat rises from 0.009 to 0.027, about 3x more often. Rarer words get more negative updates.

blocks.md: **Subsampling frequent words.** Words like *the* appear in almost every window and carry little information. The paper discards each occurrence of word $w$ during training with probability $P(w) = 1 - \sqrt{t / f(w)}$, where $f(w)$ is the word's frequency (its share of all tokens) and $t$ is a threshold, typically around $10^{-5}$. This $P(w)$ is a discard probability, not the noise distribution. Read it as keeping each occurrence with probability $\sqrt{t / f(w)}$: a word making up 5 percent of tokens is kept with probability $\sqrt{0.0002} \approx 0.014$ (since $t / f = 10^{-5} / 0.05 = 0.0002$), and a word at or below $t$ is always kept. The paper says the formula was chosen heuristically, to cut words far above $t$ hard while keeping the order of frequencies. They report it speeds up training and improves the vectors of rare words.

blocks.title: Subsampling: probability of discarding a word

scenes.caption: t = 1e-5. A word making up 5% of tokens is dropped 98.6% of the time; a word at 0.01% is dropped 68.4%. Words at or below t are always kept.
Raise t to 1e-4: the curve shifts right, so fewer words are subsampled and each is dropped less often.

blocks.md: The formula above is the one in the paper. The released word2vec C code uses a slightly different expression with a `sample` parameter, so if you are reproducing exact numbers, read the code of the implementation you use.

blocks.question: Mid-training, a negative sample $w_i$ already has $\sigma(u_{w_i}^\top v_c) = 0.01$. How much does this negative change $u_{w_i}$ in this step?
options: A lot, because negatives always get the full learning rate
Nothing, because negatives only update $v_c$
Very little, because its gradient is $0.01\, v_c$
It moves toward $v_c$, increasing the score
blocks.explain: The gradient for a negative is $s_i v_c$. When the model already gives it a tiny probability of being real, $s_i$ is near 0 and so is the update. Easy negatives teach little, which is one reason the choice of noise distribution matters.

blocks.question: Why is SGNS so much cheaper per training pair than the full softmax?
options: It uses smaller vectors
It skips the input vector update
It only trains on frequent words
It touches $k + 1$ output vectors instead of all $W$
blocks.explain: The softmax normalizer needs every output vector; the negative sampling objective needs only the true context and the k samples. With k = 5 and W = 1,000,000 that is 6 dot products instead of a million.

lessons.title: Train word2vec yourself: SGNS in PyTorch, then gensim

blocks.md: The last lesson did one update by hand. This lesson turns lessons 2 and 3 into a program that learns vectors for about 19,500 words. The corpus is [text8](https://mattmahoney.net/dc/textdata.html), the first 100,000,000 bytes of a cleaned English Wikipedia dump: lowercase words separated by single spaces, with digits spelled out. To keep the run short we use its first 10,000,000 characters, which split into 1,706,282 tokens.

blocks.code:
import collections, random, torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0); random.seed(0)
text = open('text8').read()[:10_000_000].split()  # first 10 MB of text8
counts = collections.Counter(text)
vocab = [w for w, n in counts.most_common() if n >= 5]  # min_count 5
idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
ids = [idx[w] for w in text if w in idx]
freq = torch.tensor([counts[w] for w in vocab], dtype=torch.float)
keep = (1e-4 / (freq / freq.sum())).sqrt().clamp(max=1)  # keep prob, t = 1e-4
noise = freq ** 0.75; noise /= noise.sum()              # unigram^0.75
print(len(text), 'tokens,', len(vocab), 'words')

def make_pairs(ids, c=2):  # fresh subsample each epoch, window c
    kept = [i for i in ids if random.random() < keep[i]]
    cen, ctx = [], []
    for p, w in enumerate(kept):
        for q in range(max(0, p - c), min(len(kept), p + c + 1)):
            if q != p: cen.append(w); ctx.append(kept[q])
    return torch.tensor(cen), torch.tensor(ctx)
blocks.caption: Part 1, data. Run with text8 unzipped next to the script; all three parts form one file.

blocks.md: Each line maps to an earlier idea. `min_count` 5 drops words seen fewer than 5 times, leaving 19,501 words, because a vector trained on 2 examples is mostly noise. `keep` is lesson 3's subsampling rule written as a keep probability, $\min(1, \sqrt{t / f(w)})$, with $t = 10^{-4}$ (the paper's $10^{-5}$ would discard about 77 percent of the tokens, too many to spare in a corpus of only 1.7 million). `noise` is the unigram distribution raised to 3/4. `make_pairs` subsamples afresh each epoch (one full pass over the data) and emits every (center, context) pair within $c = 2$ positions, as in lesson 2's sliding window.

blocks.code:
W, d, k = len(vocab), 100, 5
v = torch.nn.Embedding(W, d, sparse=True)  # input vectors (center)
u = torch.nn.Embedding(W, d, sparse=True)  # output vectors (context)
torch.nn.init.uniform_(v.weight, -0.5 / d, 0.5 / d)
torch.nn.init.zeros_(u.weight)             # output vectors start at 0, as in gensim
opt = torch.optim.SparseAdam([v.weight, u.weight], lr=0.003)

def sgns_loss(cen, ctx):
    B = len(cen)
    neg = torch.multinomial(noise, B * k, replacement=True).view(B, k)
    vc = v(cen)                                          # (B, d)
    pos = (u(ctx) * vc).sum(1)                           # (B,)  u_o . v_c
    negs = torch.bmm(u(neg), vc.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2) # (B, k) u_neg . v_c
    return -(F.logsigmoid(pos) + F.logsigmoid(-negs).sum(1)).mean()

def cos(a, b):
    x, y = v.weight[idx[a]].detach(), v.weight[idx[b]].detach()
    return round(float(x @ y / (x.norm() * y.norm())), 2)

def neighbours(w, n=5):
    E = F.normalize(v.weight.detach(), dim=1)
    return [vocab[i] for i in (E @ E[idx[w]]).topk(n + 1).indices[1:]]
blocks.caption: Part 2, model and loss.

blocks.md: Two `nn.Embedding` tables hold the input vectors $v$ and output vectors $u$ of lesson 2. They start the way the original word2vec C code starts them: input rows uniform in $\pm 0.5/d$ (current gensim uses $\pm 1/d$), output rows all zero, as in gensim. `sparse=True` makes the backward pass return gradients for the looked-up rows only (lesson 1), which is why the optimizer is `SparseAdam`: plain `torch.optim.Adam` raises an error on sparse gradients. `torch.multinomial` draws the negatives, and the loss line is exactly lesson 3's objective with a minus sign, averaged over a batch.

def sgns_loss(cen, ctx):
    B = len(cen)

        if step in (1, 100, 1000):
            print(step, round(loss.item(), 3), [cos(a, b_) for a, b_ in probes])
    print('epoch', epoch, step, round(loss.item(), 3), [cos(a, b_) for a, b_ in probes])
for w in ['france', 'three', 'computer']:
    print(w, neighbours(w))

lessons.title: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI

blocks.md: Trained vectors are compared with **cosine similarity**, $\cos(a, b) = a^\top b / (\lVert a \rVert \lVert b \rVert)$: the dot product divided by the product of the two vectors' lengths, which is the dot product of the two vectors after scaling each to length 1. Cosine ignores vector length and looks only at direction. Nearest neighbours under cosine are how you look up similar words, products or documents.

Mikolov et al. (2013a) found that relationships appear as roughly consistent **offsets**. To answer *man is to king as woman is to ?*, compute $x = v_{king} - v_{man} + v_{woman}$ and return the vocabulary word whose vector is closest to $x$ by cosine. The paper adds a detail that is easy to miss: *we discard the input question words during this search*.

blocks.prompt: Why would excluding the three input words matter? Guess before looking at the toy example below.
blocks.reveal: Because $x$ is usually still closest to **king** itself. Subtracting *man* and adding *woman* changes only a small gender component; everything else that makes *king* distinctive stays. Nissim et al. (2020) re-ran the standard analogy test (the 19,544 questions of Mikolov et al., 2013a, such as *Athens is to Greece as Oslo is to ?*) on the GoogleNews vectors (Google's released word2vec vectors, trained on about 100 billion words of news): accuracy (micro, pooled over all questions) was 0.74 with input words excluded and 0.21 when they were allowed, mostly because the answer came back as the second word (*king*).

blocks.title: Cosine to king - man + woman (toy 6-d vectors)

scenes.caption: Toy vectors built so the gender difference is small, as in real data. Unconstrained nearest neighbour: king (0.934) beats queen (0.766).
Exclude the input words man, king and woman, as the paper does. Now queen (0.766) wins over prince (0.672). The famous result depends on this rule.

blocks.md: Vector arithmetic analogies are a nice demo, not a law. The answer depends on excluding inputs, and Nissim et al. show that other implementation choices (casing, frequency cutoffs, the exact formula) change results too. The same arithmetic surfaces social biases: Bolukbasi et al. (2016) found that the GoogleNews word2vec vectors complete *man : computer programmer :: woman : x* with *homemaker*.

**What is SGNS actually computing?** Levy and Goldberg (2014) showed that, if $d$ is large enough for each dot product to take any value, the SGNS objective is maximized when $v_w^\top u_c = \mathrm{PMI}(w, c) - \log k$, where pointwise mutual information compares how often $w$ and $c$ co-occur with how often they would by chance (their analysis uses the empirical unigram as the noise distribution). So SGNS implicitly factorizes a **shifted PMI matrix** of word-context counts: the table of PMI minus $\log k$ for every word and context is written as the product of the input-vector table and the transposed output-vector table.

blocks.caption: PMI is the log of: the number of (w, c) pairs times the total number of pairs, over the number of times w is a center times the number of times c is a context. #(w, c): pairs with center w and context c. |D|: total pairs. #(w), #(c): how often w is a center and c a context.

blocks.md: Where the formula comes from: the probability of seeing the pair is its count divided by the total number of pairs, $\#(w, c)/|D|$. If $w$ and $c$ were independent, it would be the product of their separate probabilities: the share of pairs with center $w$, $\#(w)/|D|$, times the share of pairs with context $c$, $\#(c)/|D|$. PMI is the log of the first over the second, and the totals cancel down to the formula above. PMI 0 means the pair co-occurs exactly as often as chance predicts, and positive means more often. *Pointwise* means it is computed for one pair of values; the mutual information of two variables is this PMI averaged over all pairs, weighted by how often each pair occurs.

Why the shift by $\log k$? SGNS is a classifier of real versus noise pairs, and with free dot products its best score for a pair is the log of the odds that the pair is real. As a real pair, $(w, c)$ shows up as many times as it co-occurs. As noise, every time $w$ is a center it brings $k$ negatives, and each of them is $c$ with probability equal to $c$'s share of all contexts, so the noise count is $k$ times the count of $w$ times the count of $c$, over the total. The log of the real count over the noise count is exactly PMI minus $\log k$.

blocks.title: Pair counts #(w, c) for the 18 pairs of lesson 2

scenes.caption: Rows are center words, columns context words. Each count is a pair from the sliding window; the total over all cells is 18.
(sat, the) occurs 2 times. sat is a center 4 times and the is a context 5 times, so PMI = ln(2 x 18 / (4 x 5)) = ln 1.8 = 0.588: they co-occur 1.8x more than chance.
With k = 5, SGNS's optimum for this cell is 0.588 - ln 5 = -1.022. Cells with count 0, like (cat, mat), have PMI of minus infinity; SGNS never reaches that, it just pushes the dot product low.

blocks.md: This links prediction-based embeddings to older count-based methods, which first count co-occurrences into a big word by context table and then compress that table into short vectors with a matrix factorization. **GloVe** (Pennington et al., 2014; short for Global Vectors, because it trains on corpus-wide co-occurrence counts) fits it directly: it minimizes a weighted least-squares loss so that $w_i^\top \tilde w_j + b_i + \tilde b_j \approx \log X_{ij}$, where $w_i$ is the vector of word $i$, $\tilde w_j$ a separate context vector for word $j$ (like $u$ in skip-gram), $b_i$ and $\tilde b_j$ are learned single-number biases, and $X_{ij}$ counts co-occurrences, with weight $f(x) = (x/x_{max})^{\alpha}$ below $x_{max} = 100$ and 1 above, and $\alpha = 3/4$.

The weight $f$ is 0 for pairs that never co-occur, so the log of 0 is never needed, small for rare and noisy counts, and capped at 1 so the most frequent pairs do not dominate. Both families turn co-occurrence statistics into low-dimensional vectors.

blocks.prompt: GloVe weighs each cell by $f(X_{ij}) = (X_{ij}/100)^{3/4}$ (capped at 1). In the 18-pair count matrix above, which cells add nothing to GloVe's loss, and how much more does (sat, the), count 2, weigh than (the, cat), count 1?
blocks.reveal: The 9 zero cells add nothing, because $f(0) = 0$: GloVe trains only on pairs that occurred, which is how it avoids $\log 0$. (SGNS, by contrast, still pushes such pairs apart through its negatives.) The weights are $f(2) = 0.0532$ and $f(1) = 0.0316$, a ratio of $2^{3/4} = 1.68$: twice the count, 1.68 times the weight.

blocks.title: GloVe on the 18-pair counts: weights and targets

scenes.caption: Weights f(X) with x_max = 100 and alpha = 3/4. Count-1 cells get 0.0316 and count-2 cells 0.0532. The 9 zero cells are masked: weight 0, so they never enter the loss.
Targets log X: 0 for count 1, ln 2 = 0.693 for count 2. GloVe fits w_i . w~_j + b_i + b~_j to these values, weighted by f.
(sat, the): log X = 0.693 = PMI 0.588 + 0.105, where 0.105 = ln 4 + ln 5 - ln 18 depends only on the row and the column. The biases absorb it, so the dot product is left with PMI up to constants.

blocks.md: So the two families target nearly the same thing. Write $\log X_{ij} = \mathrm{PMI}(i, j) + \log \#(i) + \log \#(j) - \log |D|$: the last three terms depend on the row alone, the column alone, or neither. Pennington et al. make this argument themselves: a term that depends only on word $i$ can be absorbed into a bias $b_i$. GloVe's dot product therefore fits PMI up to per-word constants, while SGNS's fits PMI minus $\log k$. They differ in which cells count (GloVe skips zeros and down-weights rare pairs; SGNS samples negatives) more than in what they fit.

Static word embeddings (one fixed vector per word, whatever the sentence) encode co-occurrence statistics. Similar vectors mean *used in similar contexts*, which often but not always means *similar meaning*: antonyms like hot and cold share many contexts too.

lessons.title: Evaluating and visualizing an embedding space

blocks.md: You trained a model; is it any good? There are two kinds of answer. **Intrinsic** evaluation tests the vectors directly against human judgements, such as how similar people rate two words, or the analogy test of lesson 5. **Extrinsic** evaluation plugs the vectors into a real task, such as a sentiment classifier, and measures that task. Intrinsic tests are cheap and fast; extrinsic tests are what you actually care about.

A **word-similarity benchmark** is a list of word pairs, each with an average human rating. The model's score for a pair is its cosine. Ratings and cosines live on different scales, so the benchmark compares only their order, with **Spearman's rank correlation** $\rho$: replace each list by ranks (1 for the lowest) and correlate the ranks. $\rho = 1$ means the model orders every pair as humans do, 0 means no relation, and -1 means the reverse order. Without ties it has a short form, where $d_i$ is the rank difference of pair $i$ and $n$ is the number of pairs:

blocks.caption: Spearman's rho without ties: 1 minus 6 times the sum of squared rank differences, over n times (n squared minus 1).

blocks.title: Five SimLex-999 pairs: humans vs the gensim model

scenes.caption: Human similarity ratings from SimLex-999 (0 to 10). Ranked from lowest: bad/great 1, smart/dumb 2, old/new 3, bad/terrible 4, smart/intelligent 5.
Cosines from lesson 4's gensim model. Ranked from lowest: old/new 1, bad/great 2, smart/intelligent 3, bad/terrible 4, smart/dumb 5.
Rank differences d (human minus model): 2, 0, 2, -3, -1. The antonym smart/dumb is the biggest miss: humans rank it 2nd lowest, the model ranks it highest.

blocks.md: By hand: $\sum d_i^2 = 4 + 0 + 4 + 9 + 1 = 18$, and $n = 5$, so $\rho = 1 - 6 \cdot 18 / (5 \cdot 24) = 1 - 108/120 = 0.1$. `scipy.stats.spearmanr` gives the same 0.1 on these numbers. On these five pairs the model barely agrees with people, and one antonym pair is responsible for most of the damage.

Which pairs a benchmark contains decides what it rewards. [SimLex-999](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.3456) (Hill, Reichart and Korhonen, 2014) asked raters for *similarity* proper: antonyms like *old* and *new* score 1.58 out of 10. The older WordSim-353 told raters to treat antonyms as similar, so it measures *association* (relatedness), as SimLex's authors show. Distributional vectors encode association, because antonyms share contexts (the *cheap* and *expensive* quiz of lesson 5), so the same model scores higher on WordSim-353 than on SimLex-999. Both files ship with gensim:

For extrinsic evaluation, freeze the vectors and train a small model on top, often a linear classifier, for a task you care about. Its accuracy is the score. This is the same **linear evaluation** idea lesson 10 uses for image representations: if a linear model can read the property off the vectors, the vectors contain it in an accessible form.

To *look* at a space of 100 dimensions you must project it to 2. **PCA** (principal component analysis) is linear: it keeps the two directions along which the data varies most and drops the rest, deterministically, so distances along those axes are honest but everything else is lost. **t-SNE** (van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008) is nonlinear: it places points in 2-d so that each point's close neighbours stay close, guided by a **perplexity** parameter, loosely a guess at the number of close neighbours per point (the authors suggest 5 to 50; scikit-learn's default is 30). [UMAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03426) (McInnes et al., 2018) is a newer method with the same goal.

blocks.md: t-SNE pictures are easy to over-read. The Distill article *How to Use t-SNE Effectively* (Wattenberg, Viegas and Johnson, 2016) shows with simple data that: perplexity can change the picture completely, so look at several values; you must run until the layout stops changing; **cluster sizes mean nothing**, because t-SNE expands dense clusters and contracts sparse ones; **distances between clusters may mean nothing**; and pure random noise can show clumps at low perplexity. import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE

a = rng.normal(0, 1, (100, 2))                 # tight cluster, std 1
b = rng.normal(0, 10, (100, 2)) + [100, 0]     # wide cluster, std 10, far away

def spread(Y):  # mean distance of each cluster's points to its own centre
    return [np.linalg.norm(Y[s] - Y[s].mean(0), axis=1).mean() for s in (slice(0, 100), slice(100, 200))]
for name, Y in [('input', X), ('PCA', PCA(2).fit_transform(X))] + [
        (f't-SNE perplexity {p}', TSNE(2, perplexity=p, random_state=0).fit_transform(X)) for p in (5, 30, 50)]:
    s = spread(Y); print(f'{name:22s} wide/tight spread ratio = {s[1] / s[0]:.2f}')

lessons.title: Embeddings for IDs: categorical features, hashing and weight tying

blocks.md: Lesson 1 promised product IDs and user IDs, but so far every vector came from word contexts. Most ID embeddings in production are trained differently: they are ordinary layers of a supervised model, and the only thing that shapes them is the task loss. Guo and Berkhahn (2016) call these **entity embeddings** of categorical variables. They used them in a Kaggle competition (Kaggle is a website that hosts public machine-learning contests) on the sales data of Rossmann, a German drugstore chain (daily sales of 1,115 stores, with features such as store, day of week and German state) and placed third in the competition.

A tiny version shows the effect. Six stores, seven days: stores 0 to 2 sell 10 units on weekdays and 4 at weekends (store 1 at 1.1 times that, store 2 at 0.9), and stores 3 to 5 the reverse. Give each store and each day a 2-number embedding and predict sales as their dot product. The model is told nothing except the sales numbers.

blocks.code:
import torch
torch.manual_seed(0)
# 6 stores x 7 days. Stores 0-2 sell most on weekdays, stores 3-5 at weekends.
weekday = torch.tensor([10., 10, 10, 10, 10, 4, 4])
weekend = torch.tensor([4., 4, 4, 4, 4, 10, 10])
sales = torch.stack([weekday, 1.1 * weekday, 0.9 * weekday,
                     weekend, 1.1 * weekend, 0.9 * weekend])  # (6, 7)
store, day = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(6), torch.arange(7), indexing='ij')
store, day, y = store.flatten(), day.flatten(), sales.flatten()

S = torch.nn.Embedding(6, 2)   # one learned row per store ID
D = torch.nn.Embedding(7, 2)   # one learned row per day of week
predict = lambda s, t: (S(s) * D(t)).sum(1)   # dot product = predicted sales

def cos_matrix(E):
    E = torch.nn.functional.normalize(E.detach(), dim=1)
    return (E @ E.T).numpy().round(2)

print(cos_matrix(S.weight))
opt = torch.optim.Adam([S.weight, D.weight], lr=0.05)
for step in range(3000):
    loss = ((predict(store, day) - y) ** 2).mean()   # the task loss only
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    if step in (0, 2999): print(step, round(loss.item(), 4))
print(cos_matrix(S.weight))

After 3,000 steps of the sales loss (final loss 0.0): stores 0 to 2 have cosine 1.00 with each other, as do stores 3 to 5. No label told the model which stores are alike.
Across the groups the cosine is 0.23 with seed 0 (0.37 with seeds 1 and 2): only the grouping is determined by the data, not the exact angle between groups.

blocks.md: Stores that behave alike end up pointing the same way, as Guo and Berkhahn report at scale: their learned store embeddings place stores with similar sales close together, and a t-SNE map of the learned German-state embeddings resembles the map of Germany, although the model was never given geography. Within each group the cosine is exactly 1.00 because the rows differ only in length (1.1x, 0.9x), and cosine ignores length (lesson 5). Predicting a number as the dot product of two embeddings is a **matrix factorization**: the 6 x 7 sales table is written as a 6 x 2 store table times a 2 x 7 day table. Swap stores for users, days for items and sales for ratings, and you have the classic matrix-factorization recommender model.

blocks.prompt: Your catalog has 50 million product IDs, grows every day, and you cannot afford 50 million rows. What could you do instead of one row per ID?
blocks.reveal: Give up exact rows. Hash each ID to one of $M$ rows (the next figure), map rare IDs to a shared *unknown* row, or build the vector from features of the item. All three trade some precision for a table of fixed size.

blocks.md: The **hashing trick** (the name Weinberger et al., 2009, use for this variation on the kernel trick) skips the ID-to-row dictionary entirely: row $= h(\text{id}) \bmod M$ for a fixed hash function $h$ and a table of $M$ rows. Memory is fixed at $M \times d$, and an ID never seen before still lands on a row. The price is **collisions**: different IDs that land on the same row share one vector, and its gradient is the sum of their gradients. Weinberger et al. also use a second hash that gives each feature a random sign of +1 or -1, which makes inner products of hashed vectors unbiased: collisions add noise that averages out rather than a systematic error. That sign trick is for hashed feature vectors; the figure below uses only the plain row lookup.

blocks.title: Hashing 6 user IDs into an 8-row table

scenes.caption: Six raw IDs (user_17 written as u17). The model has no row reserved for any of them: the table has 8 rows, whatever the number of users.
Each ID is hashed (here with CRC-32, a standard checksum function) and taken mod 8: rows 7, 5, 0, 1, 5, 7. No lookup dictionary is stored.
Two collisions: u42 and u500 share row 5, u17 and u777 share row 7. Those pairs train and read the same vector. A brand-new ID also lands on some row and gets a vector at once.

blocks.tex: P(\text{an ID shares its row}) = 1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{M}\right)^{n-1} \approx 1 - e^{-n/M}
blocks.caption: With n IDs hashed uniformly into M rows, a given ID avoids every one of the other n - 1 IDs with probability (1 - 1/M) each.

blocks.code:
import zlib
M = 8                                    # rows in the hashed embedding table
for id_ in ['user_17', 'user_42', 'user_99', 'user_123', 'user_500', 'user_777']:
    print(id_, 'row', zlib.crc32(id_.encode()) % M)

def share_prob(n, M):                    # chance a given ID shares its row
    return 1 - (1 - 1 / M) ** (n - 1)
for M in (100_000, 1_000_000, 10_000_000):
    print(f'1M IDs into {M:>10,} rows: {share_prob(1_000_000, M):.3f}')

# output:
# user_17 row 7
# user_42 row 5
# user_99 row 0
# user_123 row 1
# user_500 row 5
# user_777 row 7
# 1M IDs into    100,000 rows: 1.000
# 1M IDs into  1,000,000 rows: 0.632
# 1M IDs into 10,000,000 rows: 0.095
blocks.caption: The 6-ID example and the collision formula for 1 million IDs (real output in the comments).

blocks.md: Read the last three lines as a budget. With as many rows as IDs, 63.2% of IDs share a row with someone; with 10 times as many rows, 9.5%; with a tenth as many, essentially all. At $d = 64$ in 32-bit floats (4 bytes each) those tables cost $M \times 64 \times 4$ bytes: 25.6 MB, 256 MB and 2.56 GB. Two other tools are often combined with hashing. An **unknown row** catches every ID seen fewer than some number of times, word2vec's `min_count` applied to IDs, so it is trained on all the rare IDs together. And $d$ itself is a hyperparameter: Guo and Berkhahn used 10 dimensions for 1,115 stores and 6 for the 7 days of the week.

One more trick links back to lesson 2. A language model that predicts the next word has an input embedding table and an output softmax matrix, both $W \times d$, playing the roles of $v$ and $u$. Press and Wolf (2017) recommend **weight tying**, using one matrix for both: it removes $W \times d$ parameters and lowered perplexity (a language model's standard error measure, unrelated to t-SNE's perplexity; lower is better) in the language models they tested. Their paper also reports that tying is detrimental in word2vec skip-gram, so the two tables of lesson 2 should stay separate.

An ID embedding is trained by whatever loss it feeds. Supervised losses place IDs with similar effects on the target close together. When the ID space is huge or open, trade exactness for a fixed-size table: hash, share an unknown row, or build vectors from features.

blocks.question: Your product catalog adds thousands of new item IDs every day, and the model uses one learned embedding row per ID. What problem should you expect for brand-new items?
options: Their rows are still at their random initialization because they have received no gradient, so their similarities are meaningless
None, embeddings generalize to any ID
They will all collapse to the zero vector
Their vectors will equal the average of all rows
blocks.explain: A row learns only when its ID appears in training. New IDs keep their random initial vectors (in PyTorch drawn from N(0, 1)). Systems handle this cold-start problem with a shared unknown or hashed row, or by building vectors from content features, the same idea fastText uses with character n-grams in the next lesson.

blocks.question: You hash 2 million user IDs into a table of 2 million rows. Roughly what fraction of users share their row with at least one other user?
options: About 10%
Exactly 0%, because there are as many rows as users
About 63%
About 50%
blocks.explain: With n = M the formula gives 1 - (1 - 1/M)^(M-1), about 1 - 1/e = 0.632. Equal numbers of rows and IDs do not prevent collisions, because a hash spreads IDs at random, not one per row. Ten times as many rows brings it to about 9.5%.

blocks.question: A language model has a 50,000-word vocabulary and $d = 768$. How many parameters does tying the input embedding and the output softmax matrix save?
blocks.explain: Each matrix is 50,000 x 768 = 38,400,000 numbers; tying keeps one of them. (76.8 million is the size of both together.)

lessons.title: Where word vectors fail: unseen words, many senses and bias

blocks.md: A static word table, one vector per word, fails in three predictable ways: it has nothing for a word it never saw, it gives a word with several meanings a single blended vector, and it copies whatever associations its corpus contains. This lesson shows the first two on real vectors, the third through published measurements, and the standard way to measure or reduce each.

**Unknown words.** The word2vec table has no row for a word outside its vocabulary, and lesson 4's `min_count` removed every word seen fewer than 5 times. fastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017) represents a word by its pieces instead. A character n-gram is a run of $n$ consecutive characters; fastText takes all of them for $n$ from 3 to 6, after adding `<` and `>` to mark the word's start and end, plus the whole word as one more unit. Each n-gram $g$ has its own vector $z_g$, and the skip-gram score sums over them:

blocks.caption: fastText's score for center word w and context word o: the sum, over the set G_w of n-grams in w, of the n-gram vector z_g dotted with the context word's output vector u_o (lesson 2's notation). The n-gram sum replaces w's input vector.

blocks.title: Character 3-grams of where, and of an unseen word

scenes.caption: fastText adds < and > to mark the start and end of the word, so a prefix or suffix is distinguishable from the same letters inside a word.
3-gram <wh: the first three symbols.
Sliding one symbol at a time gives whe, her, ere and re>: five 3-grams. The paper notes that her here is not the word her, which would be <her>.
where's vector is the sum of the vectors of its n-grams (n = 3 to 6 in the paper) plus one for the whole word <where>.
Suppose here never appeared in training: it has no word vector, but three of its 3-grams (her, ere, re>) were trained inside where and other words, so the sum still gives it a vector.

blocks.md: The number of possible n-grams is huge, so fastText does not keep a dictionary of them. It hashes each n-gram (with the FNV-1a hash function) into one of $K$ = 2 million rows: the hashing trick of lesson 7, collisions included. gensim implements the same model as `FastText`, with `min_n` and `max_n` for the n-gram lengths:

blocks.code:
from gensim.models import FastText
words = open('text8').read()[:10_000_000].split()
sentences = [words[i:i + 1000] for i in range(0, len(words), 1000)]
model = FastText(sentences, sg=1, vector_size=100, window=2, negative=5, sample=1e-4,
                 min_count=5, min_n=3, max_n=6, epochs=5, workers=1, seed=0)
for w in ['computerised', 'phonetically', 'goverment']:    # not in the vocabulary
    print(w, w in model.wv.key_to_index, [x for x, _ in model.wv.most_similar(w, topn=4)])
blocks.caption: fastText on the same 10 MB of text8 as lesson 4 (gensim, same settings plus n-grams of 3 to 6).

blocks.code:
computerised False ['programmed', 'computed', 'compressed', 'complied']
phonetically False ['genetically', 'specifically', 'mechanically', 'chemically']
goverment False ['regiment', 'constituent', 'punishment', 'abandonment']
blocks.caption: Output (real run, about 14 seconds). False means the word is not in the vocabulary: none of the three appeared 5 times.

blocks.md: All three unseen words get vectors, and their neighbours show what subword vectors capture: **form**. *phonetically* lands among other *-ically* adverbs, and the typo *goverment* among words ending in *-ment* (*regiment*, *punishment*) rather than near *government*. Subwords help a great deal with inflections, compounds and rare forms of known stems, but a shared suffix is not shared meaning, and a typo that breaks the stem breaks the vector.

**One vector per word.** *Bank* gets a single vector mixing every sense in the corpus, weighted by how often each occurs. In lesson 4's gensim model, the 10 nearest neighbours of *bank* are *mississippi, avenue, dakota, creek, downtown, forest, border, colorado, jutland, railroad*: all places and waterways, none financial. One sense dominated this slice of Wikipedia, and the other is invisible in the neighbour list. Contextual embeddings from Transformers, the next course, compute a fresh vector for each occurrence, so *bank* in a sentence about rivers and *bank* in a sentence about loans get different vectors.

**Bias.** Vectors reflect their corpus, including stereotypes, as lesson 5's analogy example showed. Caliskan et al. (2017) measure it with the **Word Embedding Association Test** (WEAT): take two sets of target words (say flowers and insects) and two sets of attribute words (pleasant and unpleasant), compare the average cosine of each target with each attribute set, and report an effect size in standard deviations. On GloVe vectors it reproduced the finding of the human Implicit Association Test (a reaction-time test of how readily people pair two concepts) that flowers are more pleasant than insects (effect size 1.50, against 1.35 in the human study), and it reproduced gender and race associations the same way. Bolukbasi et al. (2016) propose a mitigation: find a gender direction (for example from *she* minus *he*), and remove that component from words that should be gender-neutral, such as *nurse*, so they sit equally far from each word of a pair like *he* and *she*.

A neighbour list or a benchmark score cannot show the senses a vector has blended away or the associations it carries. Probe for them directly: look up neighbours of ambiguous words, and run association tests such as WEAT on the groups your application touches. Projection debiasing is not a cure: [Gonen and Goldberg (2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.03862) show that after it, stereotyped words still cluster together and the bias can be recovered.

blocks.question: Your fastText model gives the unseen word *unhappiness* a vector close to *happiness* and *sadness*. Which part of the model made that possible?
options: The context vectors of the words around *unhappiness* at query time
A shared unknown-word row
The n-gram vectors it shares with seen words, such as *hap*, *ness* and *ness>*, summed into a vector
The full softmax over the vocabulary
blocks.explain: An unseen word has no word vector, but its character n-grams were trained inside other words. fastText sums their vectors. At query time there is no context and no training, and an unknown row would give every unseen word the same vector.

blocks.question: A support chatbot built on static word vectors treats *Apple* the fruit and *Apple* the company identically. What does this lesson suggest?
options: Increase the vector dimension so both senses fit
Use contextual embeddings, which compute a separate vector per occurrence
Train with more negative samples
Use hierarchical softmax instead of negative sampling
blocks.explain: A static table has one row per word, so every sense shares it whatever the dimension or training objective. Contextual models compute a vector from each sentence, so the two uses differ.

lessons.title: Beyond words: autoencoders and the InfoNCE loss

blocks.md: Word vectors are one case of a general idea. Bengio, Courville and Vincent (2013) frame **representation learning** as learning transformations of the data that make it easier to extract useful information for later predictors, instead of hand-engineering features. In a trained network every hidden layer is such a representation; an embedding is simply the representation of a discrete ID.

Three common ways to get a useful representation:

- **Supervised**: train on a labelled task and reuse a late hidden layer (for example the layer before an image classifier's output).
- **Reconstruction**: an *autoencoder* compresses the input to a small code and decodes it back; the code is the representation.
- **Contrastive**: pull together representations of two views of the same thing (for example two different crops of one photo) and push apart views of different things. Skip-gram with negative sampling already does this for (word, context) pairs.

**Reconstruction**, in detail. An **autoencoder** has an encoder $f$ that maps the input $x$ to a code $h = f(x)$ and a decoder $g$ that maps the code back, and it is trained to minimize a reconstruction loss $L(x, g(f(x)))$, such as the mean squared error. Copying the input would be useless, so the code is made narrower than the input (an *undercomplete* autoencoder): to rebuild $x$ from fewer numbers, the code has to keep the most important structure of the data. Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville's *Deep Learning* notes a useful anchor: with a linear decoder and squared error, an undercomplete autoencoder learns the same subspace as PCA (lesson 6).

blocks.code:
import torch
torch.manual_seed(0)
# 200 points in 3-d that lie close to a 2-d plane, plus a little noise
a, b = torch.randn(200, 1), torch.randn(200, 1)
X = torch.cat([a + b, a - b, 0.5 * a], 1) + 0.05 * torch.randn(200, 3)
X = X - X.mean(0)                           # centre the data, as PCA does

def pca_error(X, k):
    U, S, Vh = torch.linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False)
    P = Vh[:k].T                             # top-k principal directions
    return ((X - X @ P @ P.T) ** 2).mean().item()

def autoencoder_error(X, k, steps=3000):
    enc = torch.nn.Linear(3, k)              # encoder: input to a k-number code
    dec = torch.nn.Linear(k, 3)              # decoder: code back to 3 numbers
    opt = torch.optim.Adam([*enc.parameters(), *dec.parameters()], lr=0.01)
    for _ in range(steps):
        loss = ((dec(enc(X)) - X) ** 2).mean()   # reconstruction loss
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return loss.item(), enc, dec

for k in (1, 2):
    err, enc, dec = autoencoder_error(X, k)
    print(f'code size {k}: PCA {pca_error(X, k):.4f}  linear autoencoder {err:.4f}')
print('x =', X[0].numpy().round(2), ' code =', enc(X[0]).detach().numpy().round(2),
      ' reconstruction =', dec(enc(X[0])).detach().numpy().round(2))
blocks.caption: PCA and a linear autoencoder on the same 200 points that lie close to a plane in 3-d.

blocks.code:
code size 1: PCA 0.6621  linear autoencoder 0.6621
code size 2: PCA 0.0010  linear autoencoder 0.0010
x = [-0.51 -1.52 -0.57]  code = [-1.39 -1.41]  reconstruction = [-0.53 -1.54 -0.51]
blocks.caption: Output (real run).

blocks.title: A linear autoencoder on one 3-d point

scenes.caption: The input is a point of the training data: x = [-0.51, -1.52, -0.57].
The encoder squeezes it into a 2-number code, h = [-1.39, -1.41]. The code is narrower than the input, so it cannot simply copy it.
The decoder rebuilds x-hat = [-0.53, -1.54, -0.51] from the code alone: close, because this data lies near a plane.
Training minimizes the squared difference between x-hat and x, averaged over all points. After training, the decoder is usually set aside and h is the representation.

blocks.md: The autoencoder matches PCA's error exactly, at both code sizes, without being told what PCA is. A linear autoencoder is therefore no more powerful than PCA; the point of the architecture is that nonlinear encoders and decoders can learn curved, nonlinear generalizations of it. Reconstruction has a weakness as an objective, though: it rewards keeping *every* detail needed to redraw the input, including details no downstream task needs. Contrastive objectives instead decide what to keep by saying which inputs should match.

The contrastive recipe generalizes SGNS from one negative at a time to a softmax over a set. **InfoNCE** (van den Oord et al., 2018) scores one positive among $N$ candidates ($N - 1$ negatives) with a categorical cross-entropy: a softmax over the $N$ similarity scores, with loss minus the log of the probability it gives the positive, which is binary cross-entropy extended from 2 classes to $N$. NCE stands for noise-contrastive estimation, an older method that learns by telling real data from noise samples, which is what negative sampling does.

Worked example: an anchor has cosine 0.9 with its positive and 0.6, 0.3 and -0.2 with three negatives (4 candidates, so $N = 4$ in the InfoNCE sense). Uniform guessing, probability 1/4 each, would give loss $-\ln(1/4) = \ln 4 = 1.386$. A **temperature** $\tau$ divides every similarity before the softmax, so the loss is $-\ln\big(e^{s_+/\tau} / \sum_j e^{s_j/\tau}\big)$, with $s_+$ the positive's similarity and the sum over all 4 candidates. It decides how sharply the softmax separates them. The name comes from physics, where the Boltzmann distribution divides energies by a temperature: a high temperature spreads probability evenly, a low one piles it on the best option.

blocks.title: Softmax over 4 candidates at different temperatures

scenes.caption: tau = 1: probabilities [0.381, 0.282, 0.209, 0.127]. The positive gets only 0.381 and the loss is 0.964, even though it has the highest cosine.
tau = 0.5: positive 0.51, loss 0.673. Dividing by a smaller tau stretches the gaps between similarities.
tau = 0.1: positive 0.95, loss 0.051. Among the negatives, almost all the push now goes to the hardest one (0.6, weight 0.047); the easy ones (0.002 and 0.000) get about nothing.

blocks.title: Probability of the positive vs temperature

scenes.caption: Positive at 0.9: lowering tau drives its probability toward 1 because it is the most similar candidate.

Positive at 0.5, below the hardest negative (0.6): lowering tau now drives its probability toward 0, so the loss and its gradient grow large. (The dots still mark the 0.9 case.) Low tau focuses training on hard cases.

blocks.md: InfoNCE also has a useful reading. The mutual information between two views is the average PMI from lesson 5 over their pairs: how much knowing one view tells you about the other, measured in **nats** when the log is natural (1 nat is about 1.44 bits). van den Oord et al. show that the loss is minimized when e to the score of a pair (the softmax numerator) is proportional to the density ratio $p(x \mid c)/p(x)$, how much more likely $x$ is given the context $c$ than in general. The log of that ratio is the PMI of the pair, so the best score is the PMI plus a constant: the same log-odds argument lesson 5 made for SGNS. Plugging this best possible scorer into the loss gives the bound: $\log N - L_N$ is a lower bound on the mutual information between the two views, which tightens as $N$ grows. The loss $L_N$ is never negative, so the bound can never exceed $\log N$: with $N = 4$ it certifies at most $\ln 4 = 1.386$ nats however good the encoder is. That is one reason contrastive methods like large batches.

Embeddings come from an objective, not from the lookup table. Pick the objective so that items you want close (words in the same contexts, two views of one image, a user and the items they clicked) are pushed together and everything else is pushed apart.

blocks.question: A linear autoencoder with a 2-number code, trained with squared error, reaches exactly the reconstruction error of 2-component PCA on your data. What does this tell you?
options: The autoencoder found the same 2-d subspace PCA keeps, as theory predicts for a linear decoder and squared error
The autoencoder overfit and memorized the training points
Autoencoders are always equivalent to PCA, even with nonlinear layers
The code is the same two numbers PCA would give for every point
blocks.explain: With a linear decoder and squared error, an undercomplete autoencoder spans PCA's principal subspace. It can use any basis of that subspace, so its code numbers need not equal PCA's coordinates. Nonlinear autoencoders can do more than PCA.

blocks.question: A contrastive model is trained with InfoNCE over $N = 256$ candidates per anchor. What is the most mutual information, in nats, that the bound $\log N - L_N$ can certify, however good the encoder?
blocks.explain: $L_N \ge 0$, so $\log N - L_N \le \ln 256 = 5.545$ nats (8 bits). 1.386 is $\ln 4$, the limit for 4 candidates; to certify more, use more candidates.

lessons.title: Contrastive training in practice: in-batch negatives and collapse

blocks.md: **SimCLR** (Chen et al., 2020; a Simple framework for Contrastive Learning of visual Representations) uses the InfoNCE recipe of the previous lesson for images as the *NT-Xent* loss (normalized temperature-scaled cross-entropy): two random augmentations of each image are positives, the other $2N - 2$ augmented images in the batch are negatives, and similarity is cosine divided by a **temperature** $\tau$. An augmentation is a random edit that keeps what the image shows; SimCLR uses random crops resized back, colour distortion and blur. Here $N$ counts images in the batch, not candidates: $N$ images give $2N$ views, and removing the anchor and its positive leaves $2N - 2$ negatives.

blocks.caption: NT-Xent for a positive pair (i, j), as in SimCLR: minus the log of e to the positive's scaled similarity, over the sum of the same for every other example. sim is cosine similarity; the sum runs over the other 2N - 1 examples in the batch.

blocks.md: The loss looks like one softmax per pair, but it is computed for the whole batch at once. Put the $2N$ normalized view vectors in a matrix $z$, one row each, with the two views of image $i$ in rows $2i$ and $2i+1$. Then $z z^\top$ holds every pairwise cosine; divide by $\tau$, mask the diagonal, and each row is the scores of one anchor against its $2N - 1$ candidates. The partner's column is the correct class, so the loss is ordinary cross-entropy over rows. The negatives cost nothing extra to find: they are the other images already in the batch, called **in-batch negatives**. A tiny batch with $N = 3$ images:

blocks.title: One batch, one matrix: cosines of 6 views of 3 images

scenes.caption: Images A, B, C, two augmented views each, as unit vectors in 2-d (simplified: real encoders use 128 or more dimensions). One matrix product z z^T gives all 36 cosines.
The diagonal (each view with itself, always 1) is masked: a view is never its own candidate. Each row now has 5 candidates.
Each row's positive is its partner view: (A1, A2) 0.94, (B1, B2) 0.94, (C1, C2) 0.98. The other 4 entries of the row are its in-batch negatives.
Row A1 at tau = 0.5: a 5-way softmax over 0.94, -0.5, -0.77, -0.5, -0.34, each divided by tau. The positive gets probability 0.82, so the loss is 0.201.

blocks.code:
import math, torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def nt_xent(z, tau=0.5):
    """z: (2N, d), rows 2i and 2i+1 are two views of image i."""
    z = F.normalize(z, dim=1)                  # l2-normalize: dot = cosine
    sim = z @ z.T / tau                        # (2N, 2N) all pairs in one matmul
    sim.fill_diagonal_(float('-inf'))          # a view is not its own candidate
    pos = torch.arange(len(z)) ^ 1             # partner index: 0<->1, 2<->3, ...
    return F.cross_entropy(sim, pos, reduction='none')  # one loss per row

deg = torch.tensor([10., 30, 130, 150, 250, 260])        # 3 images, 2 views each
z = torch.stack([torch.cos(deg * math.pi / 180), torch.sin(deg * math.pi / 180)], 1)
print((F.normalize(z, dim=1) @ F.normalize(z, dim=1).T).numpy().round(2))
per_row = nt_xent(z)
print(per_row.numpy().round(3), round(per_row.mean().item(), 3))
print('collapsed:', nt_xent(torch.ones(6, 2)).numpy().round(3))
blocks.caption: NT-Xent in PyTorch: one matrix product, a masked diagonal and cross-entropy. The XOR with 1 maps each row to its partner.
Output (real run): the cosine matrix, the loss for each of the 6 rows and their mean, and the loss when every view is the same vector.

blocks.md: Every row's loss is near 0.2, far below $\ln 5 = 1.609$, the loss of a uniform guess among 5 candidates: each positive is clearly the best match in its row. The mean, 0.216, is the batch loss SimCLR minimizes. The last line feeds the function six identical vectors, and every row costs exactly $\ln 5$.

blocks.prompt: Suppose you drop the negatives and train only to make the two views of each image similar, minimizing $-\cos(z_i, z_j)$ over positive pairs. What does the best encoder look like?
blocks.reveal: **It maps every input to the same vector.** Then every positive pair has cosine 1 and the loss reaches its minimum, -1, without the encoder learning anything about images. This is **collapse**. The negatives are what forbid it: under NT-Xent the collapsed encoder costs $\ln(2N - 1)$ per row (1.609 above), exactly the loss of a uniform guess, no better than chance, so the loss pushes the encoder away from it.

blocks.md: Wang and Isola (2020) split what the contrastive loss asks for into two properties of the normalized embeddings. **Alignment**: the two views of an image should map to nearby points. **Uniformity**: the embeddings of all images should spread evenly over the unit sphere, keeping as much information as possible. They show the contrastive loss optimizes both as the number of negatives grows, and define a measurable loss for each:

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}} = \mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim p_{\text{pos}}} \lVert f(x) - f(y) \rVert_2^2, \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{uniform}} = \log \mathbb{E}_{x, y \sim p_{\text{data}}} e^{-2 \lVert f(x) - f(y) \rVert_2^2}
blocks.caption: Alignment: the expected squared distance between positive pairs (their alpha = 2). Uniformity: the log of the average Gaussian potential between random pairs, with their t = 2; it is at most 0, reached when all points coincide.

blocks.title: Alignment, uniformity and NT-Xent for three 6-view batches

scenes.caption: The batch from the matrix above: positives close (alignment 0.091) and points spread round the circle (L_uniform = -1.77). NT-Xent is low, 0.216.
Collapsed: all 6 views at one point. Alignment is perfect (0) but spread is 0, the worst possible, and NT-Xent rises to ln 5 = 1.609. A positive-only loss would score this batch as perfect.
Spread out but each positive on the opposite side of the circle from its partner: alignment 4.0 (the maximum for unit vectors) and NT-Xent 3.842. Spread alone is not enough either.

blocks.md: Large batches give many negatives but cost memory. **MoCo** (He et al., 2020) keeps a **queue** of encoded examples from previous batches and uses them as negatives, so the number of negatives (65,536 in their main experiments) no longer depends on the batch size. Keys in the queue were computed several steps ago, so MoCo encodes them with a separate **momentum encoder** whose weights trail the main encoder's: $\theta_k \leftarrow m\,\theta_k + (1 - m)\,\theta_q$ with $m = 0.999$. Only the main encoder is trained by backpropagation; the slow copy keeps old and new keys consistent.

**BYOL** (Grill et al., 2020) drops negatives altogether. An *online* network, with an extra MLP called the **predictor** on top, is trained to predict a *target* network's projection of another view of the same image. The target's weights are an exponential moving average of the online weights (decay starting at 0.996), and no gradient flows into it. The authors note that collapsed solutions still exist in principle; they report that the predictor together with the slowly moving target avoids them in practice.

SimCLR reports that both $\ell_2$ normalization (dividing each vector by its length so it lies on the unit sphere, which makes the dot product equal the cosine) and a properly tuned temperature matter a lot, and that in their CIFAR-10 sweep the best of $\{0.1, 0.5, 1.0\}$ at convergence was 0.5. CIFAR-10 is a standard benchmark of 60,000 small colour images, 32 by 32 pixels, in 10 classes. Representations are scored by **linear evaluation**: freeze the encoder, train only a linear classifier on its outputs, and report that classifier's accuracy.

blocks.title: SimCLR: where the representation is taken

scenes.caption: Two random augmentations of the same image form the positive pair; the same encoder f (a ResNet, a standard convolutional image network) processes both.
The loss is computed on z = g(h), the output of a small projection head (a small MLP with one hidden layer on top of the encoder).

But the representation kept for downstream tasks is h, before the head. SimCLR found h better than z by more than 10% in linear evaluation: z is trained to ignore augmentations, so the head can drop colour or orientation, which h keeps.

blocks.md: A falling contrastive loss is not proof of a good representation: a model can solve the training task with features that transfer poorly, as SimCLR's normalization ablation shows. Track a downstream measure such as linear evaluation, and check for collapse by looking at the spread of the embeddings.

blocks.question: You train a contrastive image model with $\tau = 1$ and unnormalized dot products. The contrastive loss falls nicely, but a linear classifier trained on the representation scores poorly. Which change does SimCLR's ablation most directly support?
options: Remove the negatives so the model only sees positives
Increase tau to 10 to smooth the loss
Take the representation from z instead of h
Use cosine similarity (l2 normalization) with a tuned, smaller temperature
blocks.explain: SimCLR reports that without l2 normalization the contrastive task gets easier but the representation is worse under linear evaluation, and that a proper temperature matters too. Removing negatives invites collapse (everything maps to one point), a larger tau flattens the softmax further, and h, not z, is the better representation.

blocks.question: Which of these objectives is minimized by an encoder that maps every image to the same vector?
options: Alignment alone, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}$
NT-Xent with in-batch negatives
Uniformity, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{uniform}}$
MoCo's loss with a queue of negatives
blocks.explain: A constant encoder puts every positive pair at distance 0, the minimum of alignment. Every loss that includes negatives or a uniformity term penalizes it: NT-Xent costs ln(2N - 1) per row, and uniformity reaches its maximum, 0.

blocks.question: MoCo updates its key encoder as $\theta_k \leftarrow 0.999\,\theta_k + 0.001\,\theta_q$ instead of copying $\theta_q$ every step. Why?
options: To save memory, since the key encoder has fewer parameters
The queue holds keys encoded over many past steps, and a slowly changing key encoder keeps them comparable with new ones
Because backpropagation through the key encoder is too slow
To make the key encoder collapse to a constant
blocks.explain: Keys in the queue come from different past steps. If the key encoder changed as fast as the query encoder, old and new keys would live in inconsistent spaces. He et al. report that m = 0.999 works much better than a smaller momentum.
